ProductNames.16792: Microsoft Exchange Server Subscription Edition RTM

Notes.Title: Description
Notes.Value: Improper neutralization of input during web page generation ('cross-site scripting') in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker could send a specially crafted link to a user and persuade them to click it, with no authentication required. If a user with administrative privileges clicks the link, successful exploitation could allow the attacker to perform actions using that user's privileges, potentially allowing access to or modification of organizational data.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
According to the CVSS metric, user interaction is required (UI:R). What interaction would the user have to do?

Exploitation of the vulnerability requires that a user to open a specially crafted link.

An attacker would have no way to force users to click the link. Instead, an attacker would have to convince users to click the link through social engineering.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
According to the CVSS metric, a successful exploitation could lead to a scope change (S:C). What does this mean for this vulnerability?

The vulnerability is in the web server, but the malicious scripts execute in the victim’s browser on their machine.

CWE.Value: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

Description.Value: Publicly Disclosed:No;Exploited:No;Latest Software Release:Exploitation More Likely

Title.Value: Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

Notes.Title: Description
Notes.Value: Stack-based buffer overflow in Microsoft Exchange Server allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted email to an affected Exchange server, triggering an internal content-conversion process. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code on the server. Exploitation requires an attacker to have a deep understanding of the target environment and is not guaranteed to succeed. User interaction is not required.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to have a deep understanding of the system. Successful exploitation is not guaranteed and depends on a combination of factors that might include the environment, system configuration, and the presence of additional security measures.

Description.Value: Publicly Disclosed:No;Exploited:No;Latest Software Release:Exploitation More Likely

Title.Value: Windows Shell Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

Notes.Title: Description
Notes.Value: Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command ('command injection') in Windows Shell allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
What kind of security feature could be bypassed by successfully exploiting this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could evade Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses.

Notes.Title: FAQ
Notes.Value:
How could an attacker exploit the vulnerability?

In an email or instant message attack scenario, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file that is designed to exploit the vulnerability.

In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment.

CWE.Value: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command ('Command Injection')
